# ForgeMark

**A concurrent git push/clone throughput benchmark for any smart-HTTP git forge.**

ForgeMark measures **sustained push or clone throughput and per-operation
latency** the way an agent fleet hits a forge: many concurrent writers, readers,
or mixed sessions. It drives **real git operations** through
[`go-git`](https://github.com/go-git/go-git) (packfile build + ref update for
pushes, upload-pack for clones), so it exercises the forge paths directly — not
a synthetic HTTP approximation.

It works against **any smart-HTTP git host** — GitLab, Gitea, Bitbucket,
self-hosted, GitHub Enterprise Server, github.com, and
[Entire](https://github.com/entireio). There's no target flag: the forge is
inferred from `-remote` (and, for Entire, from the auth flags you supply).

> **Only run ForgeMark against infrastructure you own or are explicitly
> authorized to load-test.** A tight push loop is abusive traffic to a host that
> hasn't agreed to it.

## Install

```bash
go install github.com/entireio/forgemark/cmd/forgemark@latest
```

## What it measures

Per concurrency level it reports successful operations/sec,
p50/p95/p99/p99.9/max latency, and CAS-failure / error counts where they apply.
Results print as a table and are written to `results/forgemark-<id>.json` for
charting.

### Strategies

| `-strategy` | shape | what it tells you |
|---|---|---|
| `branch` (default) | N agents, **one repo**, each pushes its own branch | **Headline single-repo number.** No client-side contention (each agent owns its ref), so it isolates the server's per-repo ref-update path. |
| `repo` | N agents spread across **M repos** (`-repo-count`), own branches | Horizontal-scale ceiling — distinct repos serialize independently, so this should scale where `branch` saturates. |
| `clone` | N agents, **one repo**, each loops: **shallow-clone** the base branch → discard → repeat | Read-side ceiling: how many concurrent shallow clones/sec the forge sustains, without write load. |
| `session` | N agents, each loops: **shallow-clone** the base branch → commit+push `-session-commits` checkpoints to a fresh ephemeral branch → abandon → repeat | Realistic agent lifecycle: interleaves **read load (clone) with write load (push)** on one repo. Reports clone and push latencies separately. |

## Usage

Two steps: **set up the target repos**, then **run**.

### 1. Set up targets

ForgeMark does not create repos — it pushes to ones you provide. Create them on
your forge and make sure your credential can push:

138			// truncated measurement, not real latency.
139			if ctx.Err() != nil {

165				return fmt.Errorf("create %s: %w", name, err)
166			}
167			_, _ = rng.Read(buf) // math/rand never errors; random bytes → distinct blob

169				_ = f.Close()
170				return fmt.Errorf("write %s: %w", name, err)
171			}
172			_ = f.Close()
173			if _, err := wt.Add(name); err != nil {
174				return fmt.Errorf("add %s: %w", name, err)
175			}
176		}
177		sig := &object.Signature{
178			Name:  fmt.Sprintf("agent-%d", a.id),
179			Email: authorEmail,

197			Force:      true, // each agent owns its ref; force keeps numbers clean of spurious non-ff
198			ClientOptions: []gitclient.Option{

200				gitclient.WithHTTPAuth(auth),
201			},
202		})

204			return fmt.Errorf("push: %w", err)
205		}
206		return nil
207	}

209	// classify maps a push result to an outcome. A nil error or "already
210	// up-to-date" is success; a CAS / non-fast-forward rejection is contention;
211	// everything else is an error.
212	func classify(err error) outcome {
213		switch {
214		case err == nil, errors.Is(err, git.NoErrAlreadyUpToDate):
215			return outcomeOK
216		case errors.Is(err, git.ErrNonFastForwardUpdate):
217			return outcomeCAS
218		default:
219			msg := strings.ToLower(err.Error())
220			if strings.Contains(msg, "non-fast-forward") ||
221				strings.Contains(msg, "reference has changed") ||
222				strings.Contains(msg, "fetch first") ||
223				strings.Contains(msg, "stale info") {
224				return outcomeCAS
225			}
226			return outcomeErr
227		}
228	}

230	// maxErrMsgLen caps a retained error message. Longer messages are truncated
231	// after normalization so a long URL can't crowd the signal out of the window.

234	// reURL/reRef match the volatile substrings go-git embeds in error text — the
235	// receive-pack URL (varies by node/repo) and the destination ref (varies by
236	// agent/session). Collapsing them lets identical failures group in the results.
237	// Compiled once; the message-shape sibling of classify.
238	var (
239		reURL = regexp.MustCompile(`https?://\S+`)
240		reRef = regexp.MustCompile(`refs/heads/\S+`)
241	)
242	
243	// normalizeErr turns a raw go-git error message into a stable grouping key:
244	// collapse this run's volatile URLs/refs, then truncate. Order matters —
245	// truncating first could cut the status code that follows a long URL.
246	func normalizeErr(msg string) string {
247		if msg == "" {
248			return "(no message)"
249		}
250		msg = reURL.ReplaceAllString(msg, "<url>")
251		msg = reRef.ReplaceAllString(msg, "<ref>")
252		if len(msg) > maxErrMsgLen {
253			msg = msg[:maxErrMsgLen]
254		}
255		return msg
256	}

47	// jurisdiction token authorizes every repo the caller can reach — the data
48	// plane resolves each push live — so there's no per-repo audience and no
49	// per-repo cache. The exchange is the RFC 8693 shape: audience is the bare
50	// jurisdiction origin (e.g. https://us.example.com), scope is openid.

52		httpc    *http.Client
53		tokenURL string // core auth /oauth/token, e.g. https://us.auth.example.com/oauth/token
54		audience string // jurisdiction host bare origin, e.g. https://us.example.com
55		clientID string // public OAuth client, e.g. entire-cli

60		tok        tokenEntry

62		sf         singleflight.Group // collapses concurrent cold exchanges into one

71	// coalesce onto the same key.

76			httpc:    httpc,
77			tokenURL: tokenURL,

79			clientID: clientID,
80			subject:  subject,
81			username: username,
82		}
83	}

85	func (j *jurisdictionCreds) basicAuth(ctx context.Context, _ string) (*githttp.BasicAuth, error) {
86		token, err := j.get(ctx)
87		if err != nil {
88			return nil, err
89		}
90		// Entire ignores the username; the token is the password.
91		return &githttp.BasicAuth{Username: j.username, Password: token}, nil
92	}
93	
94	// get returns a valid jurisdiction token. A still-valid token within 2 minutes
95	// of expiry is returned immediately while a single background refresh runs
96	// (serve-stale-while-revalidate): a mid-sweep refresh must not block every
97	// agent at once, or it injects a synchronized spike into the p99/max tail this
98	// harness reports. Only a missing/expired token blocks — and singleflight
99	// collapses those concurrent first-time exchanges (all agents at startup) into
100	// one /oauth call instead of a herd.
101	func (j *jurisdictionCreds) get(ctx context.Context) (string, error) {
102		if err := ctx.Err(); err != nil {
103			return "", fmt.Errorf("jurisdiction token fetch canceled: %w", err)
104		}
105		j.mu.Lock()
106		e := j.tok
107		valid := e.token != "" && time.Now().Before(e.exp)
108		// Only a valid-but-aging token triggers an ahead-refresh. Guarding on
109		// `valid` matters: an expired token also satisfies time.Until < 2m, and
110		// setting refreshing=true here without entering the goroutine that clears
111		// it would leak the flag and permanently disable ahead-refresh.
112		startAhead := valid && time.Until(e.exp) < 2*time.Minute && !j.refreshing
113		if startAhead {
114			j.refreshing = true
115		}
116		j.mu.Unlock()
117	
118		if valid {
119			if startAhead {
120				go func() {
121					defer func() {
122						j.mu.Lock()
123						j.refreshing = false
124						j.mu.Unlock()
125					}()
126					// Best-effort: the cached token is still valid, so a failed
127					// ahead-refresh just retries on a later get; surface it but
128					// don't disrupt the sweep.
129					if _, err := j.refreshNow(); err != nil {
130						fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "forgemark: background jurisdiction-token refresh failed: %v\n", err)
131					}
132				}()
133			}
134			return e.token, nil
135		}
136		return j.refreshNow() // no valid token: block on the collapsed exchange
137	}
138	
139	// refreshNow exchanges a fresh token and caches it, with singleflight
140	// collapsing concurrent calls into one network exchange. The exchange runs on
141	// a detached, time-bounded context so a single caller's cancellation can't
142	// fail a refresh other agents are waiting on.
143	func (j *jurisdictionCreds) refreshNow() (string, error) {
144		v, err, _ := j.sf.Do(singleflightKey, func() (any, error) {
145			ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 30*time.Second)
146			defer cancel()
147			e, err := j.exchange(ctx)
148			if err != nil {
149				return "", err
150			}
151			j.mu.Lock()
152			j.tok = e
153			j.mu.Unlock()
154			return e.token, nil
155		})
156		if err != nil {
157			return "", fmt.Errorf("jurisdiction token exchange: %w", err)
158		}
159		token, ok := v.(string)
160		if !ok {
161			return "", fmt.Errorf("jurisdiction token exchange: unexpected result type %T", v)
162		}
163		return token, nil
164	}
165	
166	func (j *jurisdictionCreds) exchange(ctx context.Context) (tokenEntry, error) {
167		form := url.Values{
168			"grant_type":           {"urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange"},
169			"subject_token_type":   {"urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token"},
170			"requested_token_type": {"urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token"},
171			"subject_token":        {j.subject},
172			"audience":             {j.audience},
173			"scope":                {"openid"},
174		}
175		req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, j.tokenURL, strings.NewReader(form.Encode()))
176		if err != nil {
177			return tokenEntry{}, fmt.Errorf("build token request: %w", err)
178		}
179		req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/x-www-form-urlencoded")
180		req.SetBasicAuth(j.clientID, "") // public client: empty secret is intentional
181	
182		resp, err := j.httpc.Do(req)
183		if err != nil {
184			return tokenEntry{}, err
185		}
186		defer func() { _ = resp.Body.Close() }()
187		body, err := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 1<<20))
188		if err != nil {
189			return tokenEntry{}, fmt.Errorf("read token response: %w", err)
190		}
191		if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusOK {
192			return tokenEntry{}, fmt.Errorf("HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, strings.TrimSpace(string(body)))
193		}
194		var jr struct {
195			AccessToken string `json:"access_token"`
196			ExpiresIn   int    `json:"expires_in"`
197		}
198		if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &jr); err != nil {
199			return tokenEntry{}, fmt.Errorf("decode: %w", err)
200		}
201		if jr.AccessToken == "" {
202			return tokenEntry{}, fmt.Errorf("empty access_token")
203		}
204		ttl := jr.ExpiresIn
205		if ttl <= 0 {
206			ttl = 899 // ~15m default matching the jurisdiction-token TTL
207		}
208		return tokenEntry{token: jr.AccessToken, exp: time.Now().Add(time.Duration(ttl) * time.Second)}, nil
209	}

ForgeMark is today a CLI-only concurrent git push/clone benchmark (`cmd/forgemark`, ~2,000 lines, single `main` package). Results print as a table and land in `results/forgemark-<id>.json`. ## Phase 2 — Engine instrumentation: the Sink (B)

Design principle: the engine stays per-target and per-level; **level lifecycle is not an engine event** — the caller (CLI loop or server coordinator) calls `RunLevel` itself, so it already knows level start/end and gets `LevelResult` as the return value. The only hook the engine needs is the per-sample hot path:

```go
// Sink observes every recorded sample, including warmup samples, live.
// OnSample is called concurrently from up to `concurrency` agent goroutines
// and must be cheap and non-blocking.
type Sink interface {
    OnSample(s Sample)
}
```

Implementation: `agent` gains a `sink Sink` field; every `a.samples = append(a.samples, s)` site (5 in agent.go, 4 in session.go) is replaced by one method:

```go
func (a *agent) record(s sample) {
    a.samples = append(a.samples, s)
    if a.sink != nil { a.sink.OnSample(exportSample(s)) }
}
```

`a.samples` remains the authoritative post-hoc source for `summarize` — **CLI behavior is untouched** (nil sink, one nil-check per op, zero allocations).

**Mechanism recommendation: direct callback into a mutex-protected aggregator, not a channel.** Justification: sample rates are modest (≤ a few hundred ops/sec per target — each sample is a full git push round-trip), while a `sync.Mutex` sustains millions of lock/unlock per second even contended. The server-side sink does ~10 integer increments and one `append` to a bucket slice under the lock (<1µs). A buffered channel would need a drainer goroutine, a drop policy, and shutdown ordering, and would still allocate for batching — complexity with no payoff at this volume. No per-agent batching needed either.

`Sample` (exported): `Offset time.Duration; Dur time.Duration; Res Outcome; Op OpKind; Msg string`. Offset is relative to level start; the collector timestamps buckets itself, so no wall-clock field needed.

**Review gate:** unit test — run a fake sink through a `record`-exercising path; existing bench tests still green.

New package `internal/server` (stdlib only: `net/http`, `embed`, `encoding/json`).

### 3a. Multi-target coordination (C)

Because `RunLevel` is a synchronous fixed-duration call (`warmup+duration` timeout inside), **the level barrier is just a WaitGroup per level** — start each level simultaneously across targets, wait for all, then advance:

```go
// runmgr.go — coordinator goroutine per run
for li, c := range w.Concurrency {
    run.emit(levelStartEvent{li, c, w.Warmup, w.Duration})
    var wg sync.WaitGroup
    for _, t := range run.liveTargets() {
        wg.Add(1)
        go func(t *targetState) {
            defer wg.Done()
            t.collector.startLevel(li, time.Now())
            res, err := t.runner.RunLevel(run.ctx, c)
            if err != nil { t.dead = true; run.emit(targetErrorEvent{t.ID, li, err.Error(), true}); return }
            t.results = append(t.results, res)
        }(t)
    }
    wg.Wait()
    run.emit(levelResultEvent{...per-target results...})
    if run.ctx.Err() != nil || run.allDead() { break }
}
run.finish() // persist + run_done event
```

Alignment is exact at level start; level end skew is bounded by in-flight push completion (pushes are `PushContext`-bound, cancel promptly at the level deadline).

**Hard-error policy (recommendation): continue the others.** A target failing `NewRunner` (bad URL/auth/probe) or `RunLevel` (agent construction) is marked dead, emits a fatal `target_error` event, and is skipped in later levels; the run keeps its remaining targets — a comparison run where one forge is misconfigured still yields the other curves. The run fails as a whole only when *all* targets are dead. `NewRunner` for all targets executes concurrently in the run goroutine (the entiredb probe is a network call), so `POST /api/runs` returns immediately after validation; setup failures arrive as events.

The coordinator uses a `levelRunner` interface so the demo target (Phase 6) plugs in:

```go
type levelRunner interface {
    Label() string
    RunLevel(ctx context.Context, concurrency int) (bench.LevelResult, error)
}
```

One `RunManager` holds `map[string]*Run` under a mutex; a single active run at a time is enforced (409 on concurrent POST) — this is a load generator, overlapping runs corrupt each other's numbers. Finished runs stay in memory for the session (bounded, e.g. last 20) and on disk forever.

### 3b. Live aggregation (E)

Per target, per run — `collector.go`:

```go
type collector struct {
    mu        sync.Mutex
    levelIdx  int
    levelT0   time.Time
    cur       bucket            // counters + latencies landing in the current second
    window    [10]bucketLats    // ring of last-10s OK latencies for rolling percentiles
}
func (c *collector) OnSample(s bench.Sample)      // implements bench.Sink: increments + append, under mu
func (c *collector) snapshot(now time.Time) BucketStats // called by the 1s ticker
```

**Recommended approach: exact per-tick sort over a 10-second rolling window.** A ticker goroutine per run fires every second; for each target it locks, swaps out the current bucket, pushes its latencies into the ring, concatenates the ring (≤ 10s × few hundred ops = a few thousand float64s), sorts, and takes p50/p95/p99 with the existing `percentile()`. Sorting 3k floats is ~100µs once per second — nothing. No t-digest, no heap tricks; exact and ~40 lines. Throughput = OK count in the 1s bucket (per-second, not windowed, so spikes are visible). Buckets during warmup are emitted too (UI shades the warmup region using `level_start.warmup_sec`).

### 3c. HTTP API (D)

```

GET  /api/runs               list active + recent (redacted)

GET  /api/history            list results/*.json summaries
GET  /api/history/{file}     one parsed result doc (filename validated: no separators, must match forgemark-*.json)
GET  /                       embedded UI
```


**Credential handling (req. 6):** the wire DTO has a `Secret string` field used *only* to construct `bench.Target`; the stored `RunSpec` drops it immediately (the DTO type used for all GET responses simply has no secret field, so redaction is structural, not a filter). ### 3d. SSE event schema (D)

Standard SSE frames: `id: <seq>\nevent: <type>\ndata: <json>\n\n`, heartbeat comment every 15s. Every event appended to `run.events []event` (seq-numbered); a subscriber first receives a replay from `Last-Event-ID+1` (or 0), then live events — this makes browser reconnect and late-join free, since `EventSource` resends `Last-Event-ID` natively. Buffer is small: ~1 bucket event/sec + a handful of lifecycle events (an hour-long run ≈ 3600 events ≈ a few MB; acceptable, cap at 100k defensively).

```

data: {"run_id":"fmxyz","state":"running","started_at":"2026-07-23T10:00:00Z",
       "workload":{...as posted...},
       "targets":[{"id":0,"name":"gitlab","label":"https://gitlab.example"},
                  {"id":1,"name":"entire","label":"https://us.entire.example"}],
       "levels":[1,8,32]}

event: level_start
data: {"level_index":0,"concurrency":1,"at":"...","warmup_sec":10,"duration_sec":60}

event: bucket            // once per second while a level runs
data: {"level_index":0,"t":1784000123,
       "targets":{"0":{"ops":42,"ok":41,"cas":1,"err":0,
                       "p50_ms":88.1,"p95_ms":140.2,"p99_ms":190.0,
                       "clones":0,"clone_ok":0,"clone_err":0},
                  "1":{...}}}
       // percentiles = rolling 10s window; keys are target ids; a dead target is absent

event: level_result
data: {"level_index":0,"concurrency":1,
       "targets":{"0":{<bench.LevelResult JSON, existing tags>},"1":{...}}}

event: target_error
data: {"target":1,"level_index":0,"message":"info/refs probe: HTTP 401: ...","fatal":true}

event: run_done
data: {"state":"done","results_file":"forgemark-fmxyz.json","at":"..."}

```

All under `internal/server/static/`, embedded, zero build step, no CDN:

```
static/
  index.html          single page, hash routing (#new | #run/<id> | #history)
  css/style.css       dark dashboard theme (CSS variables, fixed 8-color target palette)
  js/app.js           router, boot
  js/api.js           fetch wrappers
  js/sse.js           EventSource wrapper (native auto-reconnect + Last-Event-ID; on run_done, close)
  js/charts.js        uPlot helpers: makeTimeChart(series-per-target), pushPoint(), aligned x-axis
  js/views/newrun.js  form: workload fields + dynamic target rows (add/remove), secret <input type=password>,
                      collapsible "entiredb" section per target, authorization checkbox (start disabled until checked),
                      github.com client-side hint + server `warnings` banner
  js/views/dashboard.js  live view: sweep progress (level i/N + per-level countdown), stat tiles per target
                      (ops/s, p95, CAS, errors), throughput chart, latency chart (percentile
                      selector p50/p95/p99, one line per target), errors+CAS chart, warmup shading
                      (uPlot band/plugin), completed-levels results table (grouped per target),
                      cancel button, target_error banners
  js/views/history.js list of /api/history entries with checkboxes → overlay comparison:
                      ops/s-vs-concurrency and p95-vs-concurrency per selected target; series
                      replay into the time charts when the doc has `series`
  vendor/uPlot.iife.min.js   (~45KB, vendored)
  vendor/uPlot.min.css
```

Streaming wiring: each chart keeps parallel arrays `[ts, ...perTargetSeries]`; a `bucket` event appends one column and calls `u.setData(data)` (uPlot handles thousands of points at 1Hz trivially). Colors assigned by target index from the fixed palette, consistent across all charts and the legend/tiles.

Reconnect: `EventSource` reconnects automatically; server replays from `Last-Event-ID`; dashboard rebuilds charts idempotently from replayed events (state derives purely from the event stream — this also makes "open dashboard mid-run" work with zero extra code).

```go

    Format   int            `json:"format"`             // 2; absent in old files
```

1. `go test ./...`

# Data Visualization

A chart is **read by people and executed by you**. This skill turns "make it look
good" into a procedure with checks, so the result is right by construction rather
than by taste.

**The method here is design-system-agnostic.** Nothing in the procedure, the form
heuristic, the six checks, or the mark specs is specific to one product. A design
system supplies a small set of *parameters* (its ramps, a categorical order, a
diverging pair, a status palette, a texture, its surfaces, its filter components);
the method consumes them unchanged. A **validated default palette** is the
reference instance, fully specified in `references/palette.md`. To target your
brand, read that file's structure and substitute its values — touch nothing else.

> The single most important habit: **the color part is computable, so compute it.**
> Never eyeball whether a palette is colorblind-safe — run `scripts/validate_palette.js`.

## The procedure — do these in order

Color comes LAST. Most bad charts pick colors first.

1. **Pick the form.** What is the data's job — magnitude, identity, polarity, a
   single headline, change-over-time? The job picks the chart type, and sometimes
   the answer is *not a chart* (a stat tile or hero number). → `references/choosing-a-form.md`
2. **Assign color by the job it does.** Categorical (identity), sequential
   (magnitude), diverging (polarity), or status (state) — each has one rule.
   Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled. → `references/color-formula.md`
3. **VALIDATE the palette — run the script, don't reason about ΔE.**
   `node scripts/validate_palette.js "<hex,hex,…>" --mode light` (relative to
   this skill's base directory — or load it as `<script type="module">` in the
   chart's own page, where it reads
   `data-palette` off `<body>` and logs a `console.table` report). It returns
   pass/fail on the lightness band, chroma floor, adjacent-pair CVD separation,
   and contrast. Fix anything that FAILs before continuing. Re-run for
   `--mode dark` with that mode's surface.
4. **Apply mark specs & spacers.** Thin marks, 4px rounded data-ends anchored to
   the baseline, 2px lines, ≥8px markers, a 2px surface gap between fills (stacked
   segments and adjacent bars alike) and a 2px surface ring on overlapping marks,
   selective direct labels. → `references/marks-and-anatomy.md`
5. **Add the hover layer — by default.** An HTML/SVG chart *is* interactive; ship
   a crosshair+tooltip on line/area and a per-mark hover tooltip on bar/dot/cell.
   The only form that skips it is a bare stat tile with no plot. Hit targets bigger
   than the mark; filters in one row above the charts. → `references/interaction.md`
6. **Final accessibility pass.** For ≥ 2 series a legend is always present and ≤ 4
   are also direct-labeled (a single series needs no legend box — the title names
   it), so identity is never color-alone; a table view exists; dark mode is **selected** — its own
   steps from the same ramps, validated against the dark surface, not an automatic
   flip; texture is available for the CVD/print/forced-colors case.
7. **Render it and look at it.** The validator checks color, not layout — open or
   screenshot the output and eyeball it for label collisions, geometry, and overflow
   before calling it done.

Then check the result against **`references/anti-patterns.md`** — it is the catalog
of what goes wrong. If your chart matches an entry, it's wrong.

## Non-negotiables (true in every design system)

- **Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled.** A 9th series is never a
  generated hue — it folds into "Other," small multiples, or composite encoding.
- **One axis.** Never a dual-axis chart (two y-scales). Two measures of different
  scale → two charts, small multiples, or indexed to a common base. *(This is the
  #1 chart mistake — see anti-patterns.)*
- **Color follows the entity, never its rank.** A filter that changes the series
  count must not repaint the survivors.
- **Sequential = one hue, light→dark. Diverging = two hues + a neutral gray
  midpoint.** Never a rainbow; never a hue at the diverging midpoint.
- **Run the validator before shipping any categorical palette.** CVD ≥ 12 is the
  target; 8–12 is a floor that is legal ONLY with secondary encoding. A contrast WARN
  obligates visible labels or a table view — it is not dismissable.
- **Thin marks; a legend always present for ≥ 2 series (none for one), with
  selective direct labels (never a number on every point); recessive grid/axes.**
- **Text wears text tokens, never the series color** — values, labels, and legends
  stay in primary/secondary/muted ink; a colored mark beside them carries identity.
- **Status colors are reserved** (good/warning/serious/critical) and never reused
  for "series 4"; they ship with an icon + label, never color alone.

## Plugging in a design system

The method is invariant; only these parameters change per system. The reference
instance — every value filled in — is `references/palette.md`.

| Parameter | What the system provides |
|---|---|
| **Ramps** | the hue scales (named steps) the palette draws from |
| **Categorical theme** | the fixed hue order (a named theme); default + alternates |
| **Sequential hue** | the default single hue for magnitude |
| **Diverging pair** | two warm/cool poles + a neutral midpoint |
| **Status palette** | good / warning / serious / critical — steps distinct from categorical |
| **Texture fill** | one directional hand-drawn fill, used at 45° / 135° |
| **Surfaces** | light & dark chart-surface colors (the validator needs these) |
| **Filter controls** | date-range & dimension controls (behavioral spec in `interaction.md`) |

To onboard a new system: fill those rows, feed its ramps to the validator, and let
it snap each slot to the nearest passing step. Structure and rules stay as written.

## Reference files

| File | What it answers |
|------|-----------------|
| `references/choosing-a-form.md` | Which chart type / is it even a chart? |
| `references/color-formula.md` | The four jobs, the six checks, snap-to-passing |
| `references/marks-and-anatomy.md` | Mark specs, spacers, labels, figures, hero number |
| `references/interaction.md` | Tooltips & hover, filters & time ranges |
| `references/components.md` | The pieces a chart is made of — build each in plain HTML |
| `references/anti-patterns.md` | **What goes wrong — check every chart against this** |
| `references/palette.md` | **The reference palette instance** — every parameter, filled in; swap for your brand's |
| `scripts/validate_palette.js` | Runnable six-checks validator (run it; don't eyeball) |

Per concurrency level it reports successful operations/sec,
p50/p95/p99/p99.9/max latency, and CAS-failure / error counts where they apply.
Results print as a table and are written to `results/forgemark-<id>.json` for
charting.

### Strategies

| `-strategy` | shape | what it tells you |
|---|---|---|
| `branch` (default) | N agents, **one repo**, each pushes its own branch | **Headline single-repo number.** No client-side contention (each agent owns its ref), so it isolates the server's per-repo ref-update path. |
| `repo` | N agents spread across **M repos** (`-repo-count`), own branches | Horizontal-scale ceiling — distinct repos serialize independently, so this should scale where `branch` saturates. |
| `clone` | N agents, **one repo**, each loops: **shallow-clone** the base branch → discard → repeat | Read-side ceiling: how many concurrent shallow clones/sec the forge sustains, without write load. |
| `session` | N agents, each loops: **shallow-clone** the base branch → commit+push `-session-commits` checkpoints to a fresh ephemeral branch → abandon → repeat | Realistic agent lifecycle: interleaves **read load (clone) with write load (push)** on one repo. Reports clone and push latencies separately. |

## Usage

Two steps: **set up the target repos**, then **run**.

### 1. Set up targets

ForgeMark does not create repos — it pushes to ones you provide. Create them on
your forge and make sure your credential can push:

- **`branch`** needs **one empty repo**.
- **`repo`** needs **M empty repos**.
- **`clone`** and **`session`** need a repo with a **base branch that has
  content** to clone. An empty repo degrades to a no-read orphan, so a read-side
  run against an unseeded repo isn't measuring what you think — push a base
  branch first.

Per forge, roughly:

```bash
# GitHub (needs the gh CLI): a throwaway private repo
gh repo create you/forgemark-target --private
# for clone/session runs, give it content:
#   git clone … && git commit --allow-empty -m base && git push

# GitLab / Gitea / self-hosted: create an empty repo in the UI or via the
# forge's API, ensure your token/user can push, and (for clone/session) push a
# base branch with at least one commit.
```

### 2. Run

Most forges just need a token. Point `-remote` at the host and supply the token
via `-token-file` (a file, or `-` for stdin):

```bash
FORGE="-remote https://git.example.com"

# Headline: single-repo throughput, sweep concurrency
# (-token-file reads a file; use "-" to pipe the token in on stdin instead)
forgemark $FORGE -token-file ~/.forge-token \
  -repos org/repo -concurrency 1,8,32 -duration 2m

# Spread across 16 repos (horizontal scale)
forgemark $FORGE -token-file ~/.forge-token -strategy repo \
  -repo-pattern "org/bench-{n}" -repo-count 16 -concurrency 32,128 -duration 2m

# Clone: read-side throughput, discard each in-memory clone (needs a seeded base branch)
forgemark $FORGE -token-file ~/.forge-token -repos org/repo \
  -strategy clone -clone-depth 1 -concurrency 8,32 -duration 2m

# Session: clone + push 5 checkpoints, abandon, repeat (needs a seeded base branch)
forgemark $FORGE -token-file ~/.forge-token -repos org/repo \
  -strategy session -session-commits 5 -clone-depth 1 -concurrency 8,32
```

The push URL is `<-remote>/<repo>` — the `-repos` value is appended **verbatim**
(ForgeMark does no path rewriting), so include a `.git` suffix if your forge
needs it. The token is used as the basic-auth password with a conventional
username (`-user` to override); most forges accept a PAT this way. The secret
comes from `-token-file` or the `ACCESS_TOKEN` env var — never a CLI flag, so it
can't leak via `ps` or shell history. Entire needs a couple of extra flags — see
below.

## Entire

Entire needs two extra flags — `-token-url` and `-jurisdiction`. Auth is a
single short-lived **jurisdiction identity token**: ForgeMark exchanges your
subject token for it (RFC 8693) and refreshes it, so one token authorizes every
repo you can reach. Pass the subject token as `-token-file`/`ACCESS_TOKEN`:

```bash
forgemark -remote https://aws-us-east-2.entire.io \
  -token-url    https://us.auth.entire.io/oauth/token \
  -jurisdiction https://us.entire.io \
  -token-file   ~/.entire-subject-token \
  -repos your/repo -concurrency 1,8,32,128 -duration 2m
```

detection to high-volume content writes; a tight push loop at high concurrency
will get throttled or blocked, and high-volume automated load testing of
github.com isn't sanctioned by their acceptable-use policy. ForgeMark detects a
`github.com` remote and warns above concurrency 16. For a higher-volume
comparison, point `-remote` at a **GitHub Enterprise Server** you control.

## Key flags

| flag | default | notes |
|---|---|---|
| `-remote` | — | base URL of the forge (e.g. `https://gitlab.com`); the cluster base URL for Entire |
| `-token-file` | — | file holding the credential secret; `-` reads stdin (else `$ACCESS_TOKEN`) |
| `-user` | `x-access-token` | basic-auth username (token forges ignore it) |
| `-repos` / `-repo-pattern`+`-repo-count` | — | target repo path(s), appended verbatim; `-repo-pattern` expands `{n}` to `1..N` |
| `-strategy` | `branch` | `branch` \| `repo` \| `clone` \| `session` |
| `-branch-prefix` | — | prepended verbatim to branch names, before the run ID (e.g. `bench/` → `refs/heads/bench/fm...`); groups branches for easy cleanup |
| `-concurrency` | `1,8,32,128` | swept sequentially, one row each |
| `-duration` / `-warmup` | `60s` / `10s` | measured window / discarded ramp |
| `-files-min`/`-files-max`/`-file-size` | `1`/`10`/`2048` | commit shape; ignored by `clone` |
| `-object-format` | `auto` | `sha1` \| `sha256`; `auto` probes the Entire advertisement (generic/github default sha1) |
| `-session-commits` | `5` | session strategy checkpoints per cloned session |
| `-clone-depth`/`-base-ref` | `1`/default | clone/session strategy knobs |
| `-insecure` | `false` | skip TLS verification (dev / self-signed hosts) |
| `-out` | — | JSON results path (default `results/forgemark-<id>.json`) |

### Entire (supplying `-token-url` + `-jurisdiction` selects it)

| flag | notes |
|---|---|
| `-token-url` | core `/oauth/token` endpoint (presence selects Entire) |
| `-jurisdiction` | jurisdiction audience host, bare origin (presence selects Entire) |
| `-client-id` | public OAuth client id (default `entire-cli`) |

In this mode `-token-file`/`ACCESS_TOKEN` carries the subject token to exchange,
not a forge PAT.

## Environment variables

| var | notes |
|---|---|
| `ACCESS_TOKEN` | the credential secret, if `-token-file` isn't given: the forge token, or Entire's subject token. `-token-file` is preferred (keeps the secret out of the environment too). |

## How it works

- **Each agent** keeps an in-memory go-git repo (object format matched to the
  remote), commits 1–10 small files per iteration, and pushes its own branch in
  a tight loop. Agents are pinned round-robin across the target's nodes.
- **Clone runs** create each shallow clone in memory and discard it after
  recording latency, so the client side stays off disk.
- **Stats**: every operation is timed; warm-up samples are dropped; exact
  percentiles are computed from the sorted OK-latency set.

## Caveats

- Run the generator **close to the target** (same region). Push latency from a
  distant machine is dominated by round-trip time, so you'd be measuring the
  network path, not the forge. Watch the generator's CPU stays below 100% at the
  top concurrency level, or it — not the server — is your bottleneck.
- `branch`/`repo` leave one per-agent branch each on the target (no cleanup);
  `session` deletes each ephemeral branch as the agent abandons it; `clone`
  does not write refs. Use throwaway repos regardless. Pass `-branch-prefix`
  (e.g. `bench/`) to namespace the branches so they're easy to find and delete
  on the target afterwards.
- `branch`/`repo` use force-push on agent-owned refs so numbers aren't polluted
  by spurious non-fast-forwards; the server still does the full receive-pack, so
  throughput is unaffected.
